extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science; scientists and educated readers interested in taxonomy/classification of the sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Provide a principled scheme for grouping and relating scientific disciplines (abstract vs concrete; precise vs synoptic; inorganic vs organic), explaining the basis (space/time discrimination, reduction to conceptual models/ideal motions, scale of corpuscles) and illustrating with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and Time as bases of classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Space is the abstract of all relations of coexistence; Time is the abstract of all relations of sequence. Sciences that deal exclusively with Space and Time (relations of coexistence and sequence) are fundamentally different from sciences that deal with the existences which Space and Time contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the perceptual modes (space and time) and their conceptual equivalents to distinguish abstract branches (logic, mathematics) from other sciences. Example: Logic and Mathematics form a class of sciences more widely unlike the rest because they deal entirely with these relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary multiplication of existences (Occam's canon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification should not introduce duplicate or superfluous entities — 'we ought not to multiply existences beyond what are necessary to account for phenomena.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parsimony when positing conceptual categories; critique of Spencer's treating space/time both as forms of perception and as 'forms of things' is cited as unnecessary duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract versus Concrete Sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two main groups: Abstract Sciences, which deal with conceptual equivalents of modes by which perception discriminates (e.g., space, time, number, logic); and Concrete Sciences, which deal with the contents of perception (phenomena themselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This primary division provides the starting-point for a classification: Abstract = concepts/modes of discrimination (logic, pure mathematics); Concrete = phenomena (physical, biological sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract sciences classified by mode of discrimination (space/time; qualitative/quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract Science may treat general relations of discrimination (applying to both time and space) or refer in particular to space or time; relations of discrimination may be qualitative (logic) or quantitative (arith., calculus, measurement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinctions such as discrete vs continuous quantity, and the special relations of space (descriptive vs metrical geometry) and time (change, kinematics) to subdivide abstract sciences. Examples include Logic/Orthology, Arithmetic/Algebra, Theory of Measurement, Calculus, Kinematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete versus continuous quantity as classification criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity may be discrete and definite (arithmetic, counts) or continuous and changing (height, temperature, speed); sciences dealing mainly with one or the other form an important subdivision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify branches (e.g., Arithmetic/Algebra for discrete; Differential and Integral Calculus, Theory of Functions for continuous) and include allied theories (errors, probability, statistics) for measurement contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise (Exact) versus Synoptic (Descriptive) Sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between sciences reduced to a complete conceptual model (Precise/Exact/Concise) and those remaining in a catalogue/description state (Synoptic/Descriptive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the extent to which synoptic classification has been replaced by brief conceptual resumes (scientific formulae or laws) as the quantitative criterion. Example: Astronomy (precise; can predict exact transit times) vs Meteorology (synoptic; only approximate predictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to ideal motions (basis for Precise Physical Sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify physical sciences according to whether phenomena have been analysed into ideal elementary motions (molecules, atoms, corpuscles) — those that can be so reduced form Precise Physical Science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied Mathematics is the link between abstract motion theory and the ideal corpuscle motions used to conceptualise inorganic phenomena. Where such reduction has not yet been achieved, the subject is Synoptic Physical Science (in process of becoming precise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base classification on vague or unfounded physical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using speculative, imprecise, or empirically unsupported principles (e.g., Spencer's 'redistribution of force') as the foundation for systematic classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A principle used to subdivide sciences must have real foundation in the relevant domain; otherwise it yields inconsistent or unhelpful groupings (example: separating Astronomy from Mechanics/Physics based on Spencer's redistribution notion is criticized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify physical sciences by scale/level of corpuscle (molar, molecular, atomic, ether)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the conceptual corpuscle level to subdivide Precise Physical Sciences: Molar Physics (motion of bodies; mechanics), Molecular Physics (relative motion of molecules; elasticity, sound, hydromechanics), Atomic Physics (motions of atoms; theoretical chemistry, spectrum analysis), Physics of the Ether (motions of ether-elements; radiation, light, heat, electricity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign subfields to the appropriate level and use the nature of the idealized particles and their motions to justify the placement; list of example subfields is provided for each level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synoptic sciences are 'Precise sciences in the making'
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat Synoptic/Descriptive Physical Sciences as those which are being gradually reduced to precise conceptual models and laws; many portions (chemistry, geology, mineralogy) are already becoming precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifications should recognize progressive refinement: a synoptic field may be largely synoptic but contain elements already formalised into laws or ideal models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundaries between branches are practical, not logical; classification is tentative
rubrics_metrics.description: When subdividing sciences the boundaries will cross and recross; topics frequently belong to more than one division, so classification schemes are empirical and tentative rather than absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect inter-relationship and continual growth; use classification as suggestive and a starting-point rather than a rigid taxonomy; avoid claiming complete logical exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify Biological Sciences by space (localisation) versus time (growth/change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subdivide biology into branches that focus on localisation/distribution (chorology, ecology, natural history) and those that focus on growth/sequence (history, evolution, biology proper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further divide growth-based studies into non-recurring (History, evolution of species, paleontology, descent of man) and recurring (Biology in narrower sense: botany, zoology); recognize that the division reflects perceptual experience and is practical rather than metaphysical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish recurring versus non-recurring growth in biological classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring growth (regular, cyclic phenomena) is treated as Biology (botany, zoology); non-recurring growth (unique historical sequences) is treated as History (evolution, paleontology, human cultural evolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical division is tied to perceptual experience; do not treat it as asserting metaphysical uniqueness of biological origins — it's a classification of observational contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify biological subfields by purpose: structure, reproduction, functions/actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Within biology distinguish morphology/histology/anatomy (form/structure), evolution/of sex/heredity/embryology (origin and development/reproduction), and physiology/psychology/sociology (functions, mental and social aspects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these functional subdivisions to place disciplines (e.g., physiology = physical side of functions; psychology = mental side; sociology = group/social products and institutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include cross-links (applied mathematics, bio-physics) between branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and classify disciplines that bridge major divisions (e.g., Applied Mathematics linking abstract motion theory to physical sciences; Bio-physics linking physical and biological sciences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some sciences serve as connective tissue between abstract/concrete or inorganic/organic domains; classification should show these links rather than force strict separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize conceptual models and brief scientific formulae over mere catalogue of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is not a mere catalogue of facts but the conceptual model by which we briefly resume our experience; the degree to which a branch has concise conceptual resumes (laws) determines its exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying, prefer groupings that reflect the availability of explanatory mechanisms or laws (e.g., law of gravitation for astronomy) rather than simple lists of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of observation and description as a classificatory requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences that require trained methods of observation and accurate description (especially organic phenomena) must be classified with attention to their observational theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific theory of observation/description is necessary for qualitative descriptions; practical training for observation (clinical clerkship, careful sketching) is recommended and informs classification of disciplines concerned with description.
